editor.title: Benedictus Richard Ricardo, on the record.
editor.lede: I work best when operations are messy and nobody's sure who's responsible for what. I come in, sort it out, and build something that holds.
body: A good system should feel obvious, not impressive. The point is that teams stop overthinking and just do the work.

automation-mandate.documentTitle: The Automation Mandate · The Operational Record
automation-mandate.metaDescription: Built reporting and SOP systems that removed 12+ hours of weekly manual work at Home Digital Indonesia.
automation-mandate.title: The Automation Mandate
automation-mandate.deck: Took a person-dependent reporting cycle and turned it into something the team could run the same way every Monday — without thinking about it.
automation-mandate.imageAlt: Operational dashboards showing weekly reporting metrics — the evidence the rebuilt cycle measured against.
automation-mandate.caption: Operational dashboards used to illustrate the weekly reporting cycle. Photograph used as illustration.
automation-mandate.lead: Three departments were losing time to the same reporting routine every week. The fix was less about software and more about giving the process real rules.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: Finance, sales, and ops were all touching the same data, reformatting the same spreadsheets, handing off the same half-finished files. It worked, technically — but it ate too much time and broke whenever someone forgot a step.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: I treated the workflow like a system, not just a spreadsheet. Rebuilt the workbook logic in Excel, wrote SOPs so the same steps happen every cycle, and mapped the whole reporting path end-to-end. The point was that anyone on the team could run it the same way every Monday without thinking.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: About twelve hours of manual work came off the weekly rhythm. But the bigger win was that people stopped dreading Mondays. The cadence was cleaner, handoffs stopped breaking, and the process could survive someone being out sick.

automation-mandate.pull: Twelve hours of manual work, gone. Replaced with a routine anyone on the team can run.
evidence: Built automated reports in Excel that took roughly 12 hours of manual work out of the weekly cycle.
Wrote shared SOPs across finance, sales, and operations so the process stopped depending on one person's memory.
Moved the work from 'someone needs to remember this' to 'this just runs now'.

impact.label: Hours saved weekly
impact.note: Manual reporting effort removed from the recurring cycle.

impact.label: Functions aligned
impact.note: Finance, sales, and operations on one structure.

impact.label: Shared routine
impact.note: Automation and SOPs combined into a repeatable weekly flow.

kpi-governance-record.metaDescription: Led 34 members across 10 divisions through a KPI rhythm at SMA Santa Maria 2.
kpi-governance-record.title: A council of thirty-four learns to keep time.
kpi-governance-record.deck: How a student presidency adopted a KPI rhythm — and started running like an institution instead of a friendship group.
kpi-governance-record.imageAlt: A speaker addresses a small audience in a workspace setting — used to illustrate institutional leadership and program design.
kpi-governance-record.caption: Leadership in a working setting — used as an illustration for institutional rhythm and program design.
kpi-governance-record.lead: A 34-member council across 10 divisions needed a better way to see what was working and what wasn't. KPIs and weekly check-ins gave us that.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: Once a student org hits 10 divisions, you can't run it on group chats and good intentions anymore. We needed a way to actually see which divisions were delivering and which were stalling.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: I introduced KPIs with weekly reviews, set clearer expectations per division, and built a stronger planning approach for school-wide programs. Nothing revolutionary — just structure where there wasn't any before.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: We could finally see what was moving and what was stuck. Programs ran more steadily, including outreach that reached twelve feeder schools. The council started operating like an institution, not a friend group.

kpi-governance-record.pull: It is easier to lead a team when the team can see what it is doing.
evidence: Ran a 34-person council across 10 divisions with KPIs and weekly check-ins.
Built institutional programs that the school itself adopted.
Led outreach campaigns that reached 12 feeder schools.

impact.label: Members led
impact.note: Leadership scope across the full organization.

impact.label: Feeder schools reached
impact.note: Scale of one major outward-facing campaign.

large-scale-event-ops.metaDescription: Live execution stable across 1,000+ attendee environments; MC-led Youth Mass 2025 for 500+ participants.
large-scale-event-ops.title: When the room is watching, the only thing visible is what fails.
large-scale-event-ops.deck: Three years of stage and backstage work for audiences of one thousand and more — and a Youth Mass for five hundred, MC-led.
large-scale-event-ops.bylineRole: Stage Coordinator & MC · Ultimate Event Organizer
large-scale-event-ops.imageAlt: Confetti falls over a crowd at a live event, illustrating the scale and timing pressure of large public programs.
large-scale-event-ops.caption: Live programs depend on transitions that hold under pressure. Photograph used as illustration.
large-scale-event-ops.lead: Live events with big audiences don't forgive sloppy transitions. My job was keeping the backstage tight enough that the audience never noticed.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: When a transition is even a little unclear, the whole room notices. The challenge in big public events isn't creating wow moments — it's making sure the boring parts (cues, pacing, handoffs) don't turn into visible failures.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: I sat right between planning and execution. My job was turning the show flow into something the tech crew, speakers, and performers could actually follow without hesitating. That meant tighter transition plans and constant communication across teams.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: Transitions ran cleaner, stage flow was more predictable, and things held even when the pressure was high. Youth Mass 2025 was probably the best proof — 500+ people, live stage, and everything stayed on time.

large-scale-event-ops.pull: When pacing holds, the event feels intentional. When it breaks, everyone notices.
evidence: Ran backstage coordination for events with 1,000+ people.
MC'd Youth Mass 2025 for 500+ participants — kept pacing tight from start to finish.
Cut down transition friction by giving every crew a clear, documented sequence.

impact.label: Audience scale
impact.note: Large live-event environments with visible execution pressure.

impact.label: Led as MC
impact.note: Youth Mass 2025 as a proof point for live communication.

vertical-rescue-ops.documentTitle: Vertical Rescue Ops · The Operational Record
vertical-rescue-ops.metaDescription: Equipment readiness, technical training, and operational discipline over 4+ active years at Vertical Rescue Indonesia.
vertical-rescue-ops.title: The quieter part of high-risk work is the part nobody films.
vertical-rescue-ops.deck: Four-plus years of equipment care and training support at Vertical Rescue Indonesia — readiness as a discipline, not a posture.
vertical-rescue-ops.lead: Readiness work doesn't get filmed. But when things go wrong in the field, it's the only thing that matters.

narrative.heading: Context
narrative.body: In technical rescue, you can't improvise once things get serious. Equipment has to be checked, training has to be consistent, and everyone needs to know their role before anyone is actually in danger.

narrative.heading: What was built
narrative.body: I took care of equipment, supported climbing sessions as lead climber and belayer, and helped keep the training standard high. Not glamorous work — just the kind that has to be right every time.

narrative.heading: Outcome
narrative.body: Equipment stayed ready. Training sessions ran more smoothly. And the people coming into the program had a better foundation before they ever hit a real situation.

vertical-rescue-ops.pull: In technical environments, confidence comes from preparation — not improvisation.
evidence: Kept equipment inspection-ready through regular maintenance.
Supported climbing and belay sessions as part of the training team.
Helped build a culture where preparation isn't optional — it's the baseline.

impact.label: Years active
impact.note: Sustained involvement in readiness and training work.

impact.label: Equipment discipline
impact.note: Inspection and maintenance as part of the standard.

impact.label: Training support
impact.note: Hands-on contribution in climbing and belay environments.
